findings.headline: Health & Social Care Pool Budget overspend of £6.4m; Local Authority contribution increased to £182.5m against £175.7m budget
findings.detail: The pooled budget with the health service shows total expenditure of £215.3m against a forecast of £208.9m. The council's own contribution rose to £182.5m from a budgeted £175.7m — a £6.8m increase. This reflects overspends in both Children's and Adults pooled services.
findings.matters: Pooled budgets can mask the council's exposure; this shows the council is bearing the cost of health service demand it cannot control. The council absorbs its share of overspends under the Section 75 agreement.
findings.figures: Pool budget overspend £6.4m; Council contribution £182.5m vs £175.7m budget (£6.8m overage)
findings.quote: Pool budget expenditure is higher than budgeted, primarily due to overspends against local authority Children's and Adults Social Care budgets addressed elsewhere in this report. Under the existing Section 75 agreement both partners are responsible for their own variation to budget and so both partners contributions have been amended to reflect the variation to budget.

findings.headline: Equalisation Reserve drawn down by £1.322m to fund in-year overspend; this is the residual after all other services' savings
findings.detail: The overall council position would have been a £4.725m overspend before reserves. Other directorates achieved £5.5m in in-year savings, leaving a net £1.322m overspend that was funded from the Equalisation Reserve. This is a one-off fix and signals that the council's baseline budget does not cover its costs.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns are not sustainable. A lender needs to know the reserve balance and trajectory; if this is a recurring pattern, reserves will be depleted and there is no buffer for unforeseen pressure.
findings.figures: £1.322m drawn from Equalisation Reserve; £5.5m in directorate savings offset £6.824m Children's Services overspend
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Revenue outturn position is a £1.322m overspend which is to be funded from the Equalisation reserve, as agreed at Budget Fixing Council in February 2026. The overspend has primarily arisen from pressures in Children's Services with an overspend position of £6.8m. This has been partially offset by savings in the other services totalling £5.5m.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £48.7m with £21.7m overspend this year; council dependent on 90% government grant to reduce it to £4.9m
findings.detail: The High Needs Block of the Dedicated Schools Grant is £22.47m overspent in 2025/26 alone. The cumulative overspend across years is £48.7m. The council has applied for a 90% High Needs Stability Grant from central government; if approved, this would reduce the liability to £4.9m, which the council will still be required to fund.
findings.matters: This is a structural deficit dependent on discretionary central government funding. If the grant is refused or cut, the council faces a material unbudgeted liability. Even with the grant, the remaining £4.9m is a commitment.
findings.figures: £48.7m cumulative; £21.727m this year; application for 90% grant to reduce to £4.9m
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant is overspent by £21.727m due continuing pressures on the High Needs Block due to increasing cost of provision and numbers of Children presenting with Special Educational Needs. The cumulative overspend position is £48.7m. Following announcements in February by Central Government an application is in progress for a 90% High Needs Stability Grant to reduce the overspend to £4.9m. The Council will be required to fund the remaining deficit.

findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £6.8m funded by drawing down the Equalisation Reserve
findings.detail: The Children's Directorate reported a final outturn overspend of £6.824m, primarily from placements (£6.134m), staffing (£0.508m), and other supported care costs. This was funded from the Equalisation Reserve as agreed in February 2026. The overspend has improved slightly since Q3 (was £7.358m) but remains a major structural pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this is temporary or recurring; funding it from reserves signals it was not absorbed by the directorate's own spending control, and the trend matters for future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £6.824m overspend; £6.134m placements; £7.358m Q3 forecast (£534k improvement)
findings.quote: An in year overspend of £6.824m was reported for the Children's Directorate. This pressure has been partially offset by in year savings across all other services, with the remaining balance of £1.322m being funded via a contribution from the Equalisation Reserve.

findings.headline: Highways governance and control weaknesses identified by internal audit
findings.detail: The Council's internal audit has identified governance and control weaknesses specifically within the highways function. These are disclosed in the AGS to strengthen compliance with the requirement to disclose governance issues and to demonstrate improvement actions being undertaken.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses represent audit risk and potential operational or financial exposure; highways is typically a material council budget and service area
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Identification of Highways governance/control weaknesses from Internal Audit

findings.headline: Chief Executive departure with interim arrangements disclosed for first time
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement includes a new disclosure of the Chief Executive departure and interim arrangements. This change reflects increased audit expectation for transparency regarding leadership stability and organisational risk during executive transitions.
findings.matters: Leadership continuity directly affects strategic execution, financial decision-making, and stakeholder confidence; lenders view management stability as a leading indicator of execution risk
findings.figures: None provided in this document
findings.quote: New disclosure of Chief Executive departure and interim arrangements

findings.paper_title: AGC Internal Audit Annual & Q4 Report
findings.headline: Data breach with information governance control improvements being implemented
findings.detail: Internal Audit reviewed a data breach incident during 2025-26. Control improvements were identified, and management has agreed and is implementing actions to strengthen data protection and information governance arrangements.
findings.matters: Data protection failures can result in regulatory penalties and fines, and indicate broader information security and governance weaknesses affecting sensitive council records.
findings.figures: One data breach incident reviewed; control improvements agreed and in progress
findings.quote: Data Breach – Internal Audit has reviewed a data breach incident during the year. Control improvements were identified, and actions have been agreed and are being implemented by management to strengthen data protection and information governance arrangements.

findings.paper_title: AGC Internal Audit Annual & Q4 Report
findings.headline: Big Help Project under Charity Commission investigation for governance and control arrangements
findings.detail: The Big Help Project has been subject to external scrutiny with the Charity Commission investigating activities linked to the organisation. Internal Audit has supported the Council in reviewing the governance and control arrangements relevant to this investigation.
findings.matters: An active investigation by an external regulator indicates control or governance failures that could have regulatory, reputational, or financial consequences.

findings.quote: Big Help Project – Matters relating to the Big Help Project have been subject to external scrutiny, with the Charity Commission investigating activities linked to the organisation. findings.headline: Highways service fraud investigation referred to police
findings.detail: Internal Audit undertook an investigation into potential fraud within the Highways service. The findings were referred to the Police, who are reviewing them to determine what further action may be needed.
findings.matters: Confirmed fraud in a major service weakens the control environment and raises questions about the accuracy of historical financial records and compliance with financial procedures.

findings.paper_title: Rochdale Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: MTFS identifies savings gaps of £2.4m for 2025/26 rising to £10.7m for 2026/27
findings.detail: Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy explicitly identifies savings gaps required to maintain balanced budgets. The £10.7m gap identified for 2026/27 represents a significant increase in savings required year-on-year. While auditor notes Council has a strong track record of delivering savings programmes, the material escalation in the gap suggests underlying structural financial pressure.
findings.matters: Growing year-on-year savings requirements indicate underlying structural financial stress that extends beyond short-term cost pressures; £10.7m is material and will require significant service changes or efficiency gains to close
findings.figures: £2.4m savings gap for 2025/26; £10.7m for 2026/27
findings.quote: The savings gaps identified in the MTFS for 2025/26 and 2026/27 are £2.4m and £10.7m respectively.

findings.paper_title: Rochdale Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £41m by 2025/26, with statutory accounting relief due to expire March 2026
findings.detail: DSG deficit was £23.4m at 31 March 2025, a £12m increase from prior year, and is forecast to reach £41m by 2025/26 with further growth projected through 2029/30. A statutory override currently shields the general fund from the deficit, but is due to expire in March 2026 (though government intends to extend to 2028). Council states it has sufficient reserves to cover the deficit if the override expires without extension, and has recovery plan in place including new school opening and participation in DfE improvement programmes.
findings.matters: Material contingent liability; if statutory relief expires without extension and is not resolved, up to £41m could impact reserves or require funding from general fund, materially affecting the Council's financial position
findings.figures: DSG deficit £23.4m at 31 March 2025 (£12m increase from prior year); forecast to rise to £41m by 2025/26; further growth anticipated to 2029/30
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025, the Council reported a DSG deficit of £23.4m, an increase of £12m from the position at the end of 2023/24. The DSG deficit is forecast to rise to £41m by 2025/26, with further growth anticipated over the MFTS period to 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Rochdale Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Children's Services demand costs forecast to overspend by £5.8m in 2025/26, quarter one already showing £3.9m overspend despite balanced budget setting
findings.detail: Council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 after closing an initial £16.8m savings gap down to £2.8m. However, quarter one financial reporting is already forecasting a full-year overspend of £3.9m, with £5.8m of that attributed to demand pressures in Children's Services alone. Auditor confirms a recovery plan is in place with identified savings to bridge the gap, but the overspend forecast represents a material miss against budget assumptions just one quarter in.
findings.matters: Early-year overspend forecasts in social care demand are a key risk indicator for councils; this suggests either budget forecasting was significantly optimistic or demand has escalated beyond prior-year patterns, both of which matter for lending decisions
findings.figures: £3.9m forecast overspend; £5.8m attributable to Children's Services demand pressure
findings.quote: We have reviewed the quarter one financial report for 2025/26 which is forecasting a £3.9m overspend for the year, this is largely because of the impact of significant demand pressures in Children's Services of £5.8m.

findings.headline: Housing emergency declared October 2023; council funding site acquisition and development in response
findings.detail: Following a housing emergency declaration in October 2023, the council is allocating £1m prudential borrowing plus £1.453m revenue contribution in 2026/27 to fund site purchases and development for housing growth.
findings.matters: A declared housing emergency signals acute local demand pressure and the choice to fund through capital rather than grants indicates this is a council priority with cost implications.
findings.figures: £1m prudential borrowing, £1.453m revenue contribution in 2026/27
findings.quote: A Housing emergency was declared in October 2023, and the project pays for sites and developments that will enable housing growth.

findings.headline: Urgent maintenance works required across 118-unit industrial property portfolio
findings.detail: The council is spending £2.039m on urgent works across its 118 commercial units spread across 10 industrial estates to bring properties to compliant and lettable standard.
findings.matters: A requirement for urgent compliance works across a large commercial portfolio suggests either poor asset management practices or aging infrastructure requiring major intervention.
findings.figures: £2.039m prudential borrowing in 2026/27
findings.quote: To carry out urgent works across the Council's industrial estates (118 units across 10 estates) to bring the units to a compliant and a standard for letting.

findings.headline: Asset maintenance backlog reduction programme commitments £4.4m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Asset Management Group scheme explicitly aims to reduce the council's maintenance backlog and bring the property portfolio up to accommodation standards, committing £4.38m in 2026/27 and £2.5m+ in subsequent years.
findings.matters: An active backlog reduction programme indicates historic underfunding of asset maintenance and signals ongoing exposure to facility deterioration if systematic investment is not maintained.
findings.quote: The scheme also aims to reduce the maintenance backlog and improve the reduced property holding to accommodation standards.

findings.headline: In-sourcing of children's residential care to control expensive external placement costs
findings.detail: The Solo Placements scheme will purchase 4 residential homes in the borough to create council-run children's homes as a replacement for expensive external provision. Investment is £900k in 2026/27 for this capital conversion.
findings.matters: A strategic move away from external placements toward internal provision indicates that external residential care costs have become unsustainable and that internal provision is expected to deliver better value.
findings.figures: £900k capital investment in 2026/27
findings.quote: They will accommodate a child in each home and create our own provision as an alternative to expensive external provisions.

findings.headline: Large property investment and development fund of £37.5m over two years with return expectations
findings.detail: The Property Growth Fund commits £32.488m Invest-to-Save plus £550k prudential borrowing in 2026/27 and £5m in 2027/28, totalling £37.5m. The scheme explicitly targets income generation and portfolio diversification alongside regeneration objectives.
findings.matters: A major debt-funded property investment programme creates ongoing debt service obligations and exposes the council to property market cycles and rental income volatility.
findings.figures: £37.5m over 2026/27–2027/28: £32.488m Invest to Save + £550k borrowing in year one, £5m in year two
findings.quote: Acquisition and development of property with the primary aims of strategic regeneration, business growth, job creation and enhancing social or economic value, with secondary aims of portfolio diversification and the achievement of a financial return in order to cover the costs of investment and provide for whole-life asset maintenance costs and future fluctuations in property investment income.

findings.headline: New school places programme heavily front-loaded at £36m with future funding uncertain and dependent on DfE allocation
findings.detail: The council is committing £36m in 2026/27 to meet statutory duty for new school places through a combination of remodelling and new builds. However, the capital plan shows zero allocation for this scheme in all subsequent years (2027/28–2030/31), and the paper notes that Department for Education funding allocations are determined annually and 'may change'.
findings.matters: A single-year commitment of this size followed by zero planned funding in subsequent years creates programme risk if DfE funding does not materialise as expected.
findings.quote: Future years funding allocations are determined by the Department for Education. These are estimated figures and may change.

findings.headline: Leopold Court hostel not currently statutory compliant; £3.3m investment required to remedy
findings.detail: The council is investing £2.129m in prudential borrowing plus £1.2m in contributions to carry out extensive repair and refurbishment at Leopold Court hostel specifically to achieve statutory compliance and return it to fit-for-purpose condition.
findings.matters: Deferred compliance on a hostel asset indicates a service failure and creates reputational and potential liability exposure for the council.
findings.figures: £2.129m prudential borrowing, £1.2m contributions in 2026/27
findings.quote: Extensive repair and refurbishment works at the hostel to reinstate the asset as statutory compliant and ensure its fit for purpose once again.

findings.headline: Springfield Park Barn cost escalation: estimated repairs rising beyond identified £2.25m survey
findings.detail: The council's condition survey identified £2.25m in required repairs at Springfield Park Barn, which is currently partly closed on health and safety grounds. However, the paper explicitly states that due to rising costs, the anticipated total is now expected to exceed this figure. Only £100k is allocated in the 2026/27 capital plan for this work.
findings.matters: A growing unfunded liability where actual costs are outpacing the original survey estimate represents either an unplanned reserve drawdown or future borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: Survey amount: £2.25m; allocated 2026/27: £100k
findings.quote: The property is in a state of disrepair with part of the building closed on health and safety grounds. A condition survey identified works required amounting to £2.25m but due to rising costs it is anticipated this amount will have increased.

findings.headline: Invest-to-save borrowing of £40m in 2026/27 assumes specific revenue savings that carry delivery risk
findings.detail: The council is borrowing £40m through the invest-to-save route in 2026/27, separate from standard prudential borrowing. This assumes that capital projects will generate sufficient revenue savings to service the debt, but the document does not detail which projects or what savings are expected.
findings.matters: Invest-to-save schemes depend on savings materialising. If projects underperform or savings fail to arrive, the council will carry the borrowing cost as permanent revenue pressure without the offsetting benefit.
findings.figures: Prudential Borrowing (Invest to Save) £40,028k in 2026/27, dropping to £5,591k in 2027/28
findings.quote: Prudential Borrowing (Invest to Save): 2026/27 budget 40,028; 2027/28 budget 5,591; 2028/29 budget 2,270; 2029/30 budget 2,290; 2030/31 budget 2,290

findings.headline: Long-term committed liability of £2.8m annually for 35 years from Rochdale Riverside head-lease
findings.detail: The council has entered a head-lease on the Rochdale Riverside retail and leisure development with a 35-year term requiring annual rental payments of £2.8m (as of 2025/26). This is recognised on the balance sheet under IFRS16 and represents a significant fixed commitment.
findings.matters: This is a long-term committed cost that constrains the revenue budget regardless of service demands or financial pressures. For a council facing budget pressure, a 35-year, £98m+ total commitment is material.
findings.figures: £2.8m annual commitment for 35-year term; Total commitment approximately £98m nominal
findings.quote: The Council has also entered into a head-lease arrangement with the owners of the Rochdale Riverside retail and leisure development located in Rochdale town centre. Through the head-lease arrangement the Council has committed to the payment of a rental sum for a term of 35 years. This annual commitment totals £2.8m in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Financing costs rising as proportion of revenue budget, now at 7.2% and heading to 7.5%
findings.detail: Interest and minimum revenue provision charges are increasing from 6.88% of net revenue stream in 2025/26 to 7.53% in 2027/28. This represents a growing share of the revenue budget consumed by debt repayment, leaving less for service delivery.
findings.matters: Lenders care about debt service capacity. As financing costs grow, they crowd out spending on services and limit the council's flexibility to address pressures.
findings.figures: Financing costs 6.88% of net revenue stream (2025/26); 7.20% (2026/27); 7.53% (2027/28)
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream: 2025/26 6.88%, 2026/27 7.20%, 2027/28 7.53%

findings.headline: Capital financing requirement increases by £45m in 2026/27, with borrowing headroom declining
findings.detail: The CFR is expected to increase by £45m during 2026/27, reaching £669.4m. Concurrently, the council's headroom within its local borrowing limit (based on 12.5% of net service expenditure) is declining from £11.6m in 2025/26 to £9.8m in 2027/28, leaving less capacity for additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A £45m increase in one year signals aggressive capital plans or invest-to-save schemes. Declining headroom means the council has less room to respond to emergencies or new capital pressures without breaching self-imposed limits.
findings.figures: CFR increase of £45m in 2026/27; Borrowing Costs Headroom £11,603k (2025/26) declining to £9,759k (2027/28); Borrowing limit 12.5% of NSE
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £45m during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Net interest costs will rise by over 13% from 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.detail: The Net Interest Budget (after Invest to Save contributions and BSR savings) grows from £6.951m to £9.148m, a jump of £2.2m or 31%. The Total Loan Interest Budget rises from £16.374m to £18.642m. This reflects both additional borrowing and the higher prevailing rates.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs compete with service funding. This trajectory affects the council's revenue budget flexibility and reserve management.
findings.figures: Net Interest Budget 2025/26 £6.951m, 2026/27 £9.148m. Total Loan Interest Budget 2025/26 £16.374m, 2026/27 £18.642m
findings.quote: Interest Cost with Internal Borrowing 6,951 9,148 9,933 10,397

findings.headline: £69m of LOBO loans may be called and refinanced at higher rates during 2026/27
findings.detail: The council holds £69m in LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loans earning an average 4.55%. If market rates rise above that, lenders will likely exercise their option to require the council to refinance at current rates. The document warns this poses 'a risk to cash flow monitoring and the consequent future need to borrow'.
findings.matters: LOBO refinancing risk is a known pressure point on council cash flow. If called in a rising rate environment, it forces immediate refinancing at market rates.
findings.figures: £69 million LOBO portfolio at average 4.55%
findings.quote: If / when market rates are above the current level being paid on those loans (average of 4.55%) the likelihood of call in is increased and the time to repay is short

findings.headline: Interest rate rises of just 1% would cost the council an additional £3.2m per year
findings.detail: The council's interest budget is highly sensitive to rate movements. A 1% rise in borrowing rates would increase annual costs by £3.2m in 2026/27 and £3.5m by 2028/29. This sensitivity grows as the council borrows more and holds less internal reserves. The treasury advisor forecasts PWLB rates staying around 3.75-4.25% depending on term.
findings.matters: Lenders care about whether a council can sustain debt if interest rates rise. Rising external borrowing combined with this rate sensitivity creates risk.
findings.quote: Additional Cost of 1% Increase 2,797 3,220 3,544 3,584

findings.headline: The council will need to borrow a further £110m over three years to fund its capital programme
findings.detail: The capital programme requires £67.9m new borrowing in 2026/27 alone, plus £23.1m in 2027/28 and £13.9m in 2028/29. This requirement exists because capital spending (£66.9m in 2026/27) exceeds available grants, contributions and capital receipts. The Underlying Borrowing Requirement rises from £487.5m to £542.6m.
findings.matters: An extra £110m of external borrowing significantly increases the council's debt service costs and market dependency. Lenders need to understand the trajectory of council debt.
findings.figures: Total capital spend via borrowing 2026/27 £67.861m, 2027/28 £23.089m, 2028/29 £13.905m. Underlying Borrowing Requirement 2025/26 £487.486m, 2026/27 £542.575m
findings.quote: the Council has a capital programme which requires funding by borrowing (totalling a further £110m from 2026/27 to 2028/29)

findings.headline: Reserves are depleting and the council will depend on external borrowing instead
findings.detail: Rochdale has historically funded capital spending from accumulated reserves, but a forward-looking balance sheet review shows these reserves declining over the next few years. As the council exhausts reserves for their intended purposes, it will need to borrow from external sources. The Internal Borrowing position (reserves used to fund capital) drops from £236.3m to £154.3m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can fund itself or whether it will become dependent on external markets. Reserve depletion marks a turning point in the council's funding resilience.
findings.quote: a forward looking balance sheet review has indicated reductions in the levels of reserves and balances over the next few years which historically have supported the internal borrowing position

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Full business rates reset from 2026/27 includes complete revaluation and baseline reset, creating significant uncertainty
findings.detail: From 2026/27, a full business rates reset will include updating business rates baselines and revaluation. Under a full reset, 'all growth accumulated to date is potentially subject to redistribution across the sector'. The council has only budgeted a £1.5m contingency for this potentially large change, and the risk is explicitly flagged as unresolved.
findings.matters: Complete reset of business rates baselines creates large downside income risk that council can only partially mitigate through contingency funds.
findings.figures: £1.5m Business Rates reset contingency budget; baseline funding from business rates reset now forms part of £208.874m Fair Funding Allocation
findings.quote: There is expected to be a significant change in our local baseline, with the income collected in 2026/27 forming part of our Fair Funding Allocation... all growth accumulated to date is potentially subject to redistribution across the sector for the forthcoming reset period.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Adult Social Care savings delivery being delayed to 2027/28, indicating execution risk on high-value targets
findings.detail: The paper notes that Adult Social Care 'have a number of high value savings in the budget for 2026/27' but 'Some of the savings will be delayed to 2027/28 to enable the service to deliver on the targets.' This suggests difficulty in delivering planned efficiencies and represents a push of pressures into future years.
findings.matters: Delay in delivering planned savings pushes pressures forward and indicates risk that full savings may not materialise, creating future budget gaps.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care savings delayed from 2026/27 to 2027/28; £1.5m delay identified in this budget
findings.quote: Adult Social Care have a number of high value savings in the budget for 2026/27. Some of the savings will be delayed to 2027/28 to enable the service to deliver on the targets.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced only through one-off reserve drawdowns and contingency releases totalling £21.1m
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget position relies heavily on one-off mitigations including £3m Collection Fund Surplus transfer, £3m Council Tax support from reserves, £2.4m Transformation Reserve contribution, £1.5m Business Rates reset contingency release, and £1m Social Care contingency release. This leaves budget gaps of £0.368m (2027/28) and £5.674m (2028/29) when one-off resources are exhausted.
findings.matters: A balanced 2026/27 budget dependent on contingency reserves and one-off drawdowns masks underlying structural deficit, with gaps emerging in forward years as these resources are exhausted.
findings.figures: £21.078m total one-off changes to budget assumptions in 2026/27; £0.368m budget gap 2027/28; £5.674m budget gap 2028/29
findings.quote: Total Changes to Budget Assumptions 21.078 [£m]... Revised Budget Gap February 2026 0.000 [2026/27], 0.368 [2027/28], 5.674 [2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review initially modelled £10m loss for Rochdale despite high deprivation ranking, offset only by active lobbying
findings.detail: Financial modelling by Pixel showed that despite Rochdale's high deprivation ranking, the Fair Funding Review reforms would deliver a cash flat settlement and reduce funding by c £10m against budgeted resources. The council only avoided this loss through explicit lobbying of MHCLG and politicians, and subsequent policy changes announced in the November Policy Statement. This represents a high level of funding uncertainty.
findings.matters: A council's funding position proved dependent on successful political lobbying rather than automatic formula, indicating a structural policy risk and that apparent fair allocation may not materialise.
findings.figures: c £10m potential funding reduction from initial Fair Funding Review modelling
findings.quote: the financial modelling provided by Pixel, the Council's external funding advisors, showed that Rochdale would receive a cash flat settlement in 2026/27, and would mean a reduction in funding against Rochdale's budgeted resources of c £10m for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Housing Benefit Subsidy shortfall growing annually with no identified funding solution
findings.detail: The level of Housing Benefit Subsidy the council can reclaim remains lower than actual costs incurred. The budget allocation notes this is 'causing increasing pressures for the Council' and is identified as a distinct risk that 'continues to grow annually'. No mitigation strategy is outlined beyond allocating funds to the service.
findings.matters: An unmeasured and growing cost gap with no policy solution at authority level indicates a structural income loss that will persist and grow.
findings.figures: Housing Subsidy Pressure budget of £0.4m (2026/27), £0.5m (2027/28), £0.6m (2028/29)
findings.quote: The level of Housing Benefit Subsidy that the Council can reclaim remains lower than the actual costs incurred. This is causing increasing pressures for the Council and funding has been allocated to help mitigate this in the service.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Social care demand growing faster than funding in both adults and children's, with risk that budget growth will not be sufficient
findings.detail: Both Adults and Children's Social Care had significant pressures in 2024/25 with additional funding allocated in 2025/26 and future years. However, pressures have continued to grow for Children's Social Care during 2025/26. The budget paper explicitly flags: 'if the increase in demand and costs continue to grow within Social Care as they have done in 2025/26, then there is a risk that the amount of Growth and funding provided in the budget from 2026/27 will not be enough to cover the costs.'
findings.matters: Structural growth in demand outpacing funding allocation suggests a recurrent problem that cannot be solved through one-off investment, creating ongoing budget volatility and potential future cuts.
findings.figures: £5.757m allocated for Children's services pressures in 2026/27; Adult Care fee inflation pressured by 6.7% Real Living Wage increase; additional £1m growth required from 2027/28
findings.quote: if the increase in demand and costs continue to grow within Social Care as they have done in 2025/26, then there is a risk that the amount of Growth and funding provided in the budget from 2026/27 will not be enough to cover the costs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £23m growing to £43m will become a permanent £1m per annum council pressure from 2028
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is currently £23m (forecast to reach £43m by March 2026) and held in an unusable reserve under statutory override expiring 31 March 2028. Government will fund 90% of the deficit as grant, but the remaining 10% (c £1m per annum) will become a local authority pressure managed through the Equalisation Reserve.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in schools funding becomes an explicit and ongoing call on council resources when the statutory override ends, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £23m current DSG deficit; forecast to increase to £43m by end of 2025/26; 10% (c £1m per annum) becomes council responsibility from 2028 onwards; 90% grant covering £38.7m of £43m forecast deficit
findings.quote: This deficit is currently held in an unusable reserve due to a statutory override, however this override is due to end on the 31st of March 2028... it is expected that the deficits for 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be funded via grant up to 90% of the deficit, the remaining 10% (c £1m per annum) will be the responsibility of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Children's services overspend of £6.7m in 2025/26 continues despite dedicated funding provision
findings.detail: The latest projected outturn for 2025/26 shows a £6.7m overspend in Children's services. The 2026/27 budget includes £5.757m to address this, with an additional social care growth reserve created to cover emerging pressures. Services are working to reduce the overspend reported at end-September, but pressures have persisted and grown despite this additional allocation.
findings.matters: Growing social care demand and cost pressures represent a structural challenge that funding allocations have not yet resolved, indicating ongoing budget management risk.
findings.figures: £6.7m overspend in Children's services (2025/26 forecast); £5.757m provision in 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: The latest projected outturn for 2025/26, which as at the end of September is a forecast overspend of £4.091m. This position includes a £6.7m overspend in Children's services

findings.headline: Council declared housing emergency in October 2023 and is deploying significant capital to address it
findings.detail: Accelerated Housing scheme allocates £2.453m (£1m borrowing plus £1.453m revenue contribution) in 2026/27, with external grants of £4.6m–£7.7m from 2028–2031 for affordable housing delivery, indicating the council recognises acute unmet housing need.
findings.matters: Declared emergencies indicate unmet local need; material capital commitments to address housing shortage affect financial planning and reflect underlying demand pressures
findings.figures: October 2023 declaration; £1,000k Prudential Borrowing, £1,453k revenue contribution 2026/27; £4,600k–£7,700k external grants 2028–2031
findings.quote: A Housing emergency was declared in October 2023, and the project pays for sites and developments that will enable housing growth.

findings.headline: Leopold Court hostel requires £2.1m in repairs to achieve statutory compliance
findings.detail: Extensive refurbishment needed to make the hostel statutory compliant and fit for purpose. £2.129m Prudential Borrowing and £1.2m contributions allocated in 2026/27, indicating the building has not been meeting required standards.
findings.matters: Assets not meeting statutory requirements must be remediated; capital for compliance is mandatory spending
findings.figures: £2,129k Prudential Borrowing, £1,200k contributions in 2026/27
findings.quote: Extensive repair and refurbishment works at the hostel to reinstate the asset as statutory compliant and ensure its fit for purpose once again.

findings.headline: Council's core intranet platform has been unsupported since April 2023
findings.detail: The intranet runs on SharePoint 2013, unsupported since April 2023. The platform is becoming difficult to develop and maintain. The council is committing capital to replacement (£933k–£712k annually 2027/28–2029/30).
findings.matters: Running unsupported software creates security and compliance risk; indicates deferred technology investment
findings.quote: The current platform on which the Intranet resides, SharePoint 2013 was unsupported from April 2023. The current intranet is becoming increasingly difficult to develop both in terms of functionality and content. There is a clear requirement for a new Intranet.

findings.headline: Council's industrial estates require urgent compliance works across 118 units
findings.detail: £2.039m in 2026/27 committed to urgent remedial works across industrial estates. The programme aims to bring units to compliant standard for letting, indicating deferred maintenance has accumulated across 10 estate locations.
findings.matters: Urgent compliance works indicate accumulated deferred maintenance; council must commit capital to meet statutory requirements
findings.figures: £2,039k in 2026/27; 118 units across 10 estates
findings.quote: To carry out urgent works across the Council's industrial estates (118 units across 10 estates) to bring the units to a compliant and a standard for letting.

findings.headline: Springfield Park Barn has unfunded maintenance liability as costs have escalated beyond original assessment
findings.detail: A condition survey identified £2.25m of required works, but the paper states costs have escalated due to rising prices. The building is in disrepair with part closed on health and safety grounds. Only £100k is allocated for developing future plans, leaving a significant gap between assessed need and available funding.
findings.matters: Unfunded capital liabilities indicate hidden costs that could impact the council's financial position and borrowing requirements
findings.figures: £2.25m original assessment anticipated to increase; £100k allocated for planning
findings.quote: The property is in a state of disrepair with part of the building closed on health and safety grounds. A condition survey identified works required amounting to £2.25m but due to rising costs it is anticipated this amount will have increased.

findings.headline: Financing costs as proportion of revenue rising to 7.53% by 2028/29, constraining service funding flexibility
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to total revenue streams is forecast to rise from 6.88% (2026/27) to 7.53% (2028/29). This shows an increasing share of revenue budget consumed by debt service, with less available for operational spending.
findings.matters: Illustrates the cumulative burden of rising external debt on the council's financial flexibility and available resources for service provision.
findings.quote: Financing Costs / Revenue Streams 6.99% 6.88% 7.20% 7.53%

findings.headline: £69m portfolio of LOBO loans at 4.55% average rate faces refinancing risk if rates remain elevated
findings.detail: Council holds £69m of historical LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loans. If market rates stay above 4.55%, lenders can call these loans with short repayment timescales, forcing council to refinance at potentially higher current rates or deplete cash reserves.
findings.matters: Creates uncontrolled refinancing risk and potential for forced borrowing at unfavorable rates, with cash flow impact on liquidity management.
findings.figures: £69 million LOBO portfolio; average rate 4.55%; current PWLB 5-year rate 3.85%, 10-year rate 4.35%
findings.quote: the increased likelihood of the Council having some of its £69 million historical portfolio of LOBO loans (Lender Option Borrower Options) called in. If / when market rates are above the current level being paid on those loans (average of 4.55%) the likelihood of call in is increased and the time to repay is short.

findings.headline: Net interest costs rising 43% by 2028/29 (£7m to £10.4m) despite Bank of England rate cuts, as debt burden grows
findings.detail: The Council's net interest budget (after internal borrowing savings) is projected to grow from £6.95m to £10.4m, a rise of £3.4m. This is driven by increasing external debt portfolio despite falling gilt yields. A 1% rise in interest rates would cost an additional £3.22m in 2026/27 alone.
findings.matters: Growing debt service burden constrains revenue budget flexibility for services and makes the council vulnerable to interest rate volatility.
findings.figures: Total Loan Interest Budget £16,374k (2025/26) → £20,048k (2028/29); Interest Cost with Internal Borrowing £6,951k → £10,397k; Additional Cost of 1% Increase £3,220k (2026/27)
findings.quote: Total Loan Interest Budget 16,374 18,642 19,858 20,048

findings.headline: Reserves being depleted as internally funded capital programme unwinds, forcing shift to external borrowing
findings.detail: The Council has financed capital by drawing down accumulated reserves rather than borrowing externally. Internal borrowing is declining from £236m to £154m. The document explicitly flags that once reserves are spent on their intended purposes, the Council must access external markets, where conditions and costs are less controllable.
findings.matters: Loss of financial buffer reduces the council's ability to absorb shocks or manage timing of borrowing, and leaves it dependent on external market conditions for future funding.
findings.figures: Internal Borrowing 2025/26 £236.3m declining to 2028/29 £154.3m; forward looking balance sheet review indicates reductions in reserves over next few years
findings.quote: As these reserves and balances are utilised for the purpose for which they were originally intended, the Council will need to borrow from external sources.

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to rise from £251m to £372m in 2026/27 alone, driven by capital programme requiring £110m over three years
findings.detail: The Council is scaling rapidly from an under-borrowed position. Capital expenditure requiring borrowing peaks at £67.9m in 2026/27, with ongoing commitments totalling £110m through 2028/29. External borrowing is projected to jump by £121m in a single year as the Council moves away from internal funding.
findings.matters: This represents a material change in the council's debt trajectory and refinancing requirements, with significant implications for financial stability and exposure to interest rate movements.
findings.figures: Opening Borrowing 2025/26 £255.1m → 2026/27 £251.2m → 2026/27 closing £372.1m; New Borrowing (Net of Maturities) £120.988m; Total Capital Spend via Borrowing £67.861m in 2026/27
findings.quote: the Council has a capital programme which requires funding by borrowing (totalling a further £110m from 2026/27 to 2028/29)

findings.headline: Available borrowing headroom declining from £11.6m to £9.8m over three years
findings.detail: The gap between the borrowing limit (12.5% of Net Service Expenditure) and budgeted borrowing costs is narrowing: from £11.603m in 2025/26 to £10.971m in 2026/27 and £9.759m in 2027/28. The council is moving closer to its borrowing ceiling, reducing capacity for additional unplanned borrowing.
findings.matters: Declining headroom indicates the council has less buffer to absorb cost overruns or additional borrowing needs if circumstances change
findings.quote: Borrowing Costs Headroom 11,603 10,971 9,759

findings.headline: Budgeted borrowing costs rising 19% over three years from £30.2m to £35.9m
findings.detail: Borrowing costs are projected at £30.225m in 2025/26, rising to £32.350m in 2026/27 and £35.947m in 2027/28. This increase of £5.7m (19%) over the period reflects either higher outstanding debt levels or exposure to interest rate movements, or both.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and suggest increasing leverage to fund the capital programme
findings.quote: Budgeted Borrowing Costs 30,225 32,350 35,947

findings.headline: Capital programme front-loaded heavily to 2026/27 with £197.6m against £28–32m baseline in other years
findings.detail: The 5-year capital programme shows 2026/27 requiring £197.6m in capital expenditure, compared to £32.4m, £28.6m, £31.3m and £31.1m in the following four years respectively. This 6-fold spike in capital investment in the first year is not explained in this document, which references the detailed capital programme being reported separately to Cabinet.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand what is driving such a large acceleration of capital investment and whether it is deliverable and appropriately funded
findings.quote: The proposed capital programme for 2026/27 to 2030/31 is as follows: Total Requirement 197,604 32,380 28,583 31,346 31,078

findings.headline: Tactical delay of long-term borrowing pending rate falls
findings.detail: The council is deliberately minimising long-term fixed borrowing and using short/medium-term options instead, betting that rates will fall further. This creates refinancing risk if rates don't fall as projected.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasting risk; the council's debt profile and future refinancing costs depend on this timing bet.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The borrowing strategy for 2026/27 will be to minimise long term fixed loans as far as possible, utilising shorter term and medium term options from other local authorities or the PWLB.

findings.headline: Investment income falling 35% as interest rates decline
findings.detail: Budgeted investment income drops from £2,396k in 2025/26 to £1,557k in 2026/27 (a loss of £839k), as the council expects interest rates to continue falling. The council notes rates 'are expected to continue to gradually fall through the period covered by this report.'
findings.matters: This reduces non-service income during a period when the council is increasing external borrowing, tightening financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Investment income 2025/26 £2,396k; 2026/27 £1,557k
findings.quote: Interest rates have reduced but still remain relatively high in response to inflationary pressures, but have reduced over the past year and are expected to continue to gradually fall through the period covered by this report.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing reserves are depleting; council moving to external debt
findings.detail: The council has funded capital expenditure with internal balances for years, but this policy is ending. Internal borrowing falls from £236m (2025/26) to £170m (2026/27), while external borrowing rises from £251m to £372m. The council explicitly acknowledges this shift is 'temporary' and that reserves 'will ultimately be used for the purpose for which they were intended or to support the overall budget.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know when a council's cheap internal funding runs out and it becomes dependent on external debt markets, changing the financial risk profile.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £236,328k (2025/26) to £170,430k (2026/27); projected borrowing £251,158k to £372,145k
findings.quote: The Council is therefore likely to externalise some of this internal borrowing in the period covered by this report and combined with an extensive capital programme funded via new borrowing, it is likely that the Council will need to take on new external borrowing in the reasonably near future.

findings.headline: Rephasing of £12m capital borrowing produces short-term revenue savings that reverse sharply into future years
findings.detail: Rephasing and reductions to the capital programme save £671k in revenue costs for 2026/27. However, the council explicitly states that 'the rephasing element of this is a short-term benefit, the costs are pushed into future years' and the revenue saving drops 77% in 2027/28 (to £164k), indicating these are deferred costs, not real reductions.
findings.matters: The 2026/27 budget relief is illusory. Revenue costs deferred, not avoided. This pushes budget pressure into future years and, combined with inflation, likely makes the medium-term financial position harder.
findings.figures: £671k saving in 2026/27; £164k in 2027/28 (77% reduction); £12m of borrowing rephased to future years
findings.quote: Rephasing and reductions to the capital programme, have reduced the revenue impact of borrowing by circa £671k in 2026/27, it is worth noting that the rephasing element of  this is a short -term benefit , the costs are pushed into future years, hence the revenue impact drops 77% in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council deploying £5m of reserves to absorb capital programme costs in 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.detail: The council is using reserves to fund shorter-life capital schemes rather than borrowing. While this produces revenue savings of £345k in 2026/27 by avoiding long-term borrowing repayment, it depletes the council's financial buffer. Reserves are typically held to manage emergencies or unexpected spending; using them to fund ongoing capital suggests constrained financial headroom.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves to manage capital pressures indicates the council lacks other solutions (borrowing headroom, external funding certainty) and reduces its ability to respond to future financial shocks.
findings.figures: £5m reserves deployed; £345k revenue saving in 2026/27; £800k per annum future saving
findings.quote: The use of £5m of reserves to fund shorter life schemes has resulted in reduced revenue costs of £345k in 2026/27, with further increased savings across future years  of £800k.

findings.headline: £20m affordable housing scheme and multiple other schemes depend on external funding not yet confirmed
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £53.041m (27% of 2026/27 budget) funded from 'Other Grants' and assumes external funding that is explicitly stated as still 'subject to clarification from Government and other sources and in some cases may involve bids for funds'. Externally funded schemes cannot start until funding is confirmed; if funding is not received, projects must be cancelled or reprised at lower cost.
findings.matters: Substantial capital schemes are contingent on external decisions outside the council's control. Delayed or lost grants force either capital programme cuts or additional unplanned borrowing.
findings.figures: £53.041m from Other Grants (27%); £57.849m from Government Grants (30%); combined £110.890m (56% of 2026/27 programme)
findings.quote: Some of the assumed external funding included in the programme is still subject to clarification from Government and other sources and in some cases may involve bids for funds. It is therefore recommended that all approvals are subject to confirmation of funding allocations.

findings.headline: External borrowing costs rising faster than budget, with no certainty on interest rate trajectory
findings.detail: The council budgeted lower PWLB rates but actual borrowing costs have risen. Total budgeted borrowing cost increases from £23.2m in 2025/26 to £25.0m in 2026/27. The council notes rates 'remain higher for longer due to ongoing high inflation' and is attempting to mitigate by delaying external borrowing and using internal cash, but this depends on maintaining sufficient liquid reserves.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs compress the revenue budget for service delivery and make future years harder to balance. This is not a one-off issue but an ongoing pressure that could worsen if rates fall more slowly than forecast.
findings.figures: £23.2m (2025/26 borrowing cost); £25.0m (2026/27); current borrowing £294m against operational boundary £663m
findings.quote: The current cost of external borrowing is higher than budgeted due to interest rates remaining higher for longer due to ongoing high inflation, however rates are forecast to reduce over the next 12 months.

findings.headline: Cabinet-approved £24.779m affordable housing scheme has only £4.779m identified funding, leaving £20m unresolved
findings.detail: Cabinet approved an affordable housing initiative of £24.779m in August, but the council has only identified £4.779m of funding (from reserves and existing budgets). The document states the council is 'currently identifying other sources of capital funding for the remaining £20m'. This represents 10% of the total 2026/27 capital programme and is not yet formally included in the capital budget.
findings.matters: An approved capital scheme with a £20m funding gap cannot proceed at the approved scale. Either the council will borrow more than currently projected or the scheme will be scaled back or delayed, both of which are material to financial planning.
findings.figures: £24.779m approved; £4.779m funded; £20m gap
findings.quote: In August, Cabinet approved a £24.779m budget , subject to funding being identified,  to address Affordable Housing, which will be added into the capital programme. Of this, £4.779m will be funded from reserves and existing budgets. The Council is currently identifying other sources of  capital funding for the remaining £20m.

findings.headline: £40.929m of Invest to Save borrowing in 2026/27 assumes unguaranteed income generation and cost reductions
findings.detail: The council classifies £40.929m of the 2026/27 borrowing as 'Invest to Save', meaning the revenue cost is supposed to be offset by income or savings generated by the schemes themselves. The council explicitly acknowledges this assumption is 'not guaranteed and is monitored carefully'. If schemes underperform, the full borrowing cost would fall to the revenue budget, creating a material budget gap.
findings.matters: This represents 21% of the capital programme but lacks certainty of revenue offset. A lender cannot treat unproven scheme returns as reliable mitigation for debt risk.
findings.figures: £40.929m (Invest to Save) in 2026/27, compared to £31.060m traditional prudential borrowing
findings.quote: The Invest to Save Schemes included in the Programme assume that the cost of borrowing will be covered by income generation or savings, however this is not guaranteed and is monitored carefully.

findings.paper_title: Append. 1 for Capital Programme for Consultation 2026/27-2030/31
findings.headline: Council pursuing major £37.5m property acquisition strategy with explicit secondary aim of generating investment returns
findings.detail: The Property Growth Fund allocates £32.5m (marked 'Invest to Save') in 2026/27 and £5m in 2027/28 for 'acquisition and development of property'. The scheme documentation states secondary aims include 'portfolio diversification and the achievement of a financial return in order to cover the costs of investment'—signalling the council is making a material real estate investment bet.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council is making a significant property market bet to generate returns needed to cover investment costs. If property values weaken or occupancy shortfalls emerge, the council's ability to service associated debt may be affected.
findings.figures: £32,488k Invest to Save + £550k prudential borrowing (2026/27); £5,000k Invest to Save (2027/28)
findings.quote: with secondary aims of portfolio diversification and the achievement of a financial return in order to cover the costs of investment

findings.paper_title: Append. 1 for Capital Programme for Consultation 2026/27-2030/31
findings.headline: Affordable housing capital investment of £4.6–£7.7m for 2028–2031 committed but unfunded
findings.detail: Rochdale's affordable housing programme (to 'accelerate delivery through strategic partnerships and modern construction methods') shows capital requirements of £4.6m in 2028/29 and £7.7m each in 2029/30–2030/31. All of this is marked 'External Funding to be Identified'—committed in principle but with no secured source.
findings.matters: Commitments without secured funding risk either non-delivery of the scheme or unplanned reallocation of internal funds away from other priorities if external sources do not materialise.
findings.figures: £4,600k (2028/29), £7,700k (2029/30), £7,700k (2030/31)—all marked 'External Funding to be Identified'
findings.quote: External Funding to be Identified

findings.paper_title: Append. 1 for Capital Programme for Consultation 2026/27-2030/31
findings.headline: Major asset repair at Springfield Park Barn already experiencing cost escalation beyond initial £2.25m survey estimate
findings.detail: A condition survey identified £2.25m of works needed at Springfield Park Barn (a community hostel). The budget explicitly flags cost inflation risk: 'Due to rising costs it is anticipated this amount may increase.' Current provision is £100k borrowing and £12,963k external grants—incomplete funding if costs rise further.
findings.matters: This signals a major asset repair under active inflationary pressure with only partial external funding secured. Further escalation forces either unplanned borrowing or incomplete delivery of essential repairs.
findings.figures: Condition survey need: £2.25m; Current funding: £100k prudential borrowing + £12,963k external grants
findings.quote: A condition survey has identified works required amounting to £2.25m. Due to rising costs it is anticipated this amount may increase.

findings.paper_title: Append. 1 for Capital Programme for Consultation 2026/27-2030/31
findings.headline: School capital condition funding faces explicit risk of reduction from ongoing academy conversions
findings.detail: The Schools Capital Condition Programme (£3.3m–£1.8m annually) is warned to face potential funding cuts if schools convert to independent status. The council acknowledges that 'Academy conversions may reduce the Department for Education allocation in future years', indicating this is a known vulnerability in its schools infrastructure funding.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know this funding stream is vulnerable to decisions by individual schools rather than council control, and that ongoing conversions will progressively reduce capacity to maintain school buildings.
findings.figures: Schools Capital Condition Programme: £3,308k (2026/27), declining to £1,808k (2027/28–2030/31)
findings.quote: Academy conversions may reduce the Department for Education allocation in future years.

findings.paper_title: Append. 1 for Capital Programme for Consultation 2026/27-2030/31
findings.headline: £36m school place provision programme entirely dependent on continued Department for Education funding allocation decisions
findings.detail: Rochdale is committing £36m in 2026/27 to provide new school places through 'internal remodeling, new build or demountable classroom units'. However, the council explicitly notes that future funding is determined externally and 'may change', with zero allocation planned for 2027/28 onwards despite ongoing demographic pressures.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether this represents a one-time investment or if the council will face unfunded service obligations if the DfE cuts or suspends allocations. Full dependency on external government decisions is a material risk.
findings.quote: Future years funding allocations determined by the Department for Education. These are estimated figures and may change.

findings.headline: Rising labour and building material costs creating scheme delivery risk across capital programme
findings.detail: The council identifies that 'increased cost of labour and building materials is having an impact on overall scheme costs and hence the delivery of schemes within the current programme'. This suggests budgeted costs may be insufficient, creating scope for overspend or scheme delays.
findings.matters: If schemes cost more than budgeted, the council will need to find additional funding, defer schemes, or reduce scope — all of which affect stated capital plans and may require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The economic climate such as increased cost of labour and building materials is having an impact on overall scheme costs and hence the delivery of schemes within the current programme and approved budget.

findings.headline: Significant capital programme relies on external funding still subject to government confirmation
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes that 'Some of the assumed external funding included in the programme is still subject to clarification from Government and other sources'. External grants and contributions total £110.890m in 2026/27 alone (56% of total programme). This creates execution risk.
findings.matters: If external funding does not materialise as forecast, the council must either reduce scheme scope, find alternative funding, or increase borrowing/draw reserves, all of which affect stated capital plans.
findings.figures: 2026/27 external funding: £57.849m government grants + £53.041m other grants + £9.311m contributions = £120.201m out of £196.844m (61%)
findings.quote: Some of the assumed external funding included in the programme is still subject to clarification from Government and other sources and in some cases may involve bids for funds. It is therefore recommended that all approvals are subject to confirmation of funding allocations.

findings.headline: Invest-to-save schemes do not guarantee revenue offset, creating unmitigated downside risk
findings.detail: The council commits to borrowing for schemes classified as 'invest to save' assuming these will generate sufficient revenue or savings to cover borrowing costs. However, the document explicitly states this 'is not guaranteed and is monitored carefully'. If schemes fail, the full borrowing cost is added to future budgets.
findings.matters: If invest-to-save schemes underperform, the council faces additional unbudgeted revenue costs that must be accommodated within an already stretched MTFS, potentially forcing difficult choices on service delivery.
findings.figures: 2026/27 invest-to-save borrowing: £40.929m
findings.quote: The Invest to Save Schemes included in the Programme assume that the cost of borrowing will be covered by income generation or savings, however this is not guaranteed and is monitored carefully.

findings.headline: £72m of new borrowing in 2026/27 (£31.060m prudential + £40.929m invest-to-save) to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The capital programme is heavily dependent on borrowing: £31.060m direct prudential borrowing and £40.929m classified as 'invest to save'. This represents a significant long-term commitment to debt repayment. The council remains below its 12.5% debt exposure policy limit at circa 10%, but the trajectory is concerning.
findings.matters: Borrowing this scale locks in long-term debt servicing commitments (typically 11-40 year repayment periods) and the 'invest to save' classification assumes income/savings will materialise, which is explicitly noted as not guaranteed.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital: £196.844m; Prudential Borrowing: £31.060m; Prudential Borrowing (Invest to Save): £40.929m; revenue cost ~10% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Capital Programme includes Schemes totalling £31.060m to be funded from Prudential Borrowing, £1.987m of which are new additions to the programme

findings.headline: Borrowing cost for 2026/27 increasing to £25.0m from £23.2m in 2025/26 due to higher interest rates
findings.detail: Annual borrowing repayment costs are rising sharply. The council notes that the current cost of external borrowing is higher than budgeted because 'interest rates remaining higher for longer due to ongoing high inflation'. Rates are forecast to reduce, but this adds pressure to revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs reduce resources available for service delivery and increase the carrying cost of the capital programme, potentially making future borrowing more difficult to sustain.
findings.quote: The total budgeted cost of borrowing for 2025/26 is £23.2m, increasing to £25.0m in 2026/27. The current cost of external borrowing is higher than budgeted due to interest rates remaining higher for longer due to ongoing high inflation

findings.headline: £20m affordable housing funding to be identified, leaving a gap in a £24.779m approved programme
findings.detail: Cabinet approved a £24.779m affordable housing budget with only £4.779m funded from reserves and existing budgets. The remaining £20m has no identified funding source. The council is 'currently identifying other sources of capital funding' for this material gap.
findings.matters: A £20m funding gap on an already-approved scheme suggests the council's ambitions exceed its ability to fund them, and delivery will depend on securing external funding that may not materialise or may come with conditions.
findings.figures: £24.779m affordable housing approved; £4.779m funded; £20m to be identified
findings.quote: The Council is currently identifying other sources of capital funding for the remaining £20m.

findings.headline: £5m of council reserves to be spent on capital schemes to offset borrowing costs
findings.detail: The council plans to use £5m of reserves in 2025/26 and 2026/27 to fund capital schemes rather than borrow, to reduce long-term borrowing repayments. While this generates £800k annual savings in debt repayment costs, it depletes the reserves that councils typically preserve for emergencies or unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves to fund capital spending signals the council is managing tight cash or revenue constraints and reduces financial flexibility to handle unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.figures: £5m of reserves to fund capital schemes; reduces annual revenue cost by circa £0.800m per annum
findings.quote: £5m of reserves will be used to fund Capital Schemes in 2025/26 and 2026/27 to reduce the ongoing cost of borrowing repayments. This will reduce the annual revenue cost by circa £0.800m per annum.

findings.headline: Rephasing of schemes generates £671k saving in 2026/27 that drops 77% in 2027/28 as costs return
findings.detail: The council moved capital schemes into future years to save £671k in 2026/27. However, the council explicitly notes: 'the rephasing element of this is a short-term benefit, the costs are pushed into future years', with the saving falling to £164k in 2027/28. This is budget timing management, not structural improvement.
findings.matters: The headline improvement masks a cliff-edge in 2027/28 when deferred costs arrive. The revenue budget gap will widen sharply when these schemes spend, creating pressure in years 2 and 3 of the MTFS.
findings.figures: £671k saving 2026/27; £164k saving 2027/28 (77% fall); similar pattern 2028/29
findings.quote: it is worth noting that the rephasing element of this is a short-term benefit, the costs are pushed into future years, hence the revenue impact drops 77% in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council deploying £5m of reserves in 2025/26-2026/27 to reduce borrowing repayment costs
findings.detail: The council is using £5m of reserves to fund capital schemes in order to avoid borrowing, thereby saving £345k in 2026/27 and rising to £800k by 2028/29 in borrowing costs. This trade-off—reserves for debt-cost reduction—suggests the council prioritises near-term revenue budget balance over maintaining reserve resilience.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits the council's buffer for unexpected pressures. Using reserves to smooth borrowing costs indicates the council is under cash pressure and betting its flexibility on the assumption that reserve levels can be rebuilt.
findings.quote: To mitigate the increased cost of the new capital bids and inflationary pressures in future years, £5m of reserves will be used to fund Capital Schemes in 2025/26 and 2026/27 to reduce the ongoing cost of borrowing repayments.

findings.headline: £40.9m of borrowing (44% of 2026/27 programme) depends on 'Invest to Save' schemes delivering promised income or savings
findings.detail: Of £196.844m total capital programme, £40.929m is classified as 'Invest to Save', meaning the council assumes these schemes will generate income or cost savings to offset the debt repayment costs. The document acknowledges this assumption 'is not guaranteed and is monitored carefully'. If schemes under-deliver, the full borrowing cost flows to the revenue budget as an unplanned burden.
findings.matters: Invest-to-save schemes carry execution risk. Underperformance immediately becomes a revenue budget pressure that is difficult to absorb. The cautious language ('monitored carefully') suggests the council has concerns about delivery.
findings.figures: £40.929m Invest to Save; £31.060m pure prudential borrowing; total borrowing £71.989m of £196.844m
findings.quote: The borrowing classed as 'Invest to save' are included within the MTFS and longer-term financial sustainability calculations as having income / budget reductions to offset the borrowing costs... If invest to save schemes do not achieve the offset, the prudential borrowing costs are added to the budget requirement in the MTFS.

findings.headline: Interest rate risk is already materialising, forcing management actions mid-programme
findings.detail: The document explicitly states: 'the current cost of external borrowing is higher than budgeted due to interest rates remaining higher for longer due to ongoing high inflation'. The council is responding by deferring external borrowing and using internal balances. While rates are 'forecast to reduce over the next 12 months', this is an assumption not yet proven.
findings.matters: Higher-than-budget borrowing costs have already arrived. If interest rate forecasts prove wrong, the revenue budget pressure will be worse than currently assumed, narrowing the council's ability to handle unexpected costs.
findings.figures: 2025/26 cost £23.2m vs budget unknown; 2026/27 cost £25.0m; forecast assumes rate reduction
findings.quote: The current cost of external borrowing is higher than budgeted due to interest rates remaining higher for longer due to ongoing high inflation, however rates are forecast to reduce over the next 12 months.

findings.headline: £20m funding shortfall on flagship £24.8m affordable housing programme remains unidentified
findings.detail: In August 2025, Cabinet approved £24.779m for affordable housing. Only £4.779m is funded from reserves and existing budgets. The remaining £20m (45% of the scheme cost) has no identified funding source. This represents 20% of the total 2026/27 capital programme and cannot proceed without funding confirmation.
findings.matters: A major approved programme has no confirmed funding mechanism. Either funding will be found (potentially through additional borrowing not yet budgeted) or the programme will shrink, signalling the council's difficulty absorbing strategic initiatives.
findings.figures: £24.779m approved; £4.779m funded; £20m gap; total 2026/27 programme £196.844m
findings.quote: The Council is currently identifying other sources of capital funding for the remaining £20m.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs rising and approaching council's self-imposed ceiling as capital programme expands
findings.detail: Borrowing costs increasing from £23.2m (2025/26) to £25.0m (2026/27). Current total borrowing cost is approximately 10% of net revenue budget, with the council's policy ceiling set at 12.5%. The council notes that interest rates are already higher than budgeted, forcing mitigation through delayed external borrowing and use of internal balances.
findings.matters: Limited headroom to the 12.5% ceiling means the council is approaching the boundary of its own risk tolerance for debt affordability, constraining future borrowing capacity and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £23.2m (2025/26) to £25.0m (2026/27); ~10% of net revenue budget; 12.5% policy ceiling
findings.quote: The revenue cost of the current proposed programme along with historic borrowing commitments is circa 10% of the forecast net revenue budget over the next 5 years.
